'''Joan Elisabeth Lowther Murray''' ({{nee|'''Clarke'''}}; 24 June 1917 – 4 September 1996) was an English [[cryptanalyst]] and [[numismatist]] who worked as a [[Cryptanalysis|code-breaker]] at [[Bletchley Park]] during the [[Second World War]]. Although she did not personally seek the spotlight, her role in the [[Cryptanalysis of the Enigma|Enigma project]] that decrypted the [[Nazi Germany|German]] secret communications earned her awards and citations, such as appointment as a [[Member of the Order of the British Empire]] (MBE), in 1946.<ref name="bbc">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-29840653|title=Joan Clarke, woman who cracked Enigma cyphers with Alan Turing|work=BBC News|date=2014-11-10|last1=Miller|first1=Joe|archive-date=10 November 2014|access-date=21 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110140239/https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-29840653|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="MBE">{{London Gazette|issue=37412|page=290 |supp=y|date=28 December 1945}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Joan Elisabeth Lowther Clarke was born on 24 June 1917 in [[West Norwood]], London, England. She was the youngest child of Dorothy Elisabeth Clarke (née Fulford) and the London [[clergyman]] [[The Reverend|Revd]]. William Kemp Lowther Clarke.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=Allyn |date=2017-03-01 |title=100 Years Ago: Joan Clarke |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/201703/rnoti-p252.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=64 |issue=03 |pages=252–255 |doi=10.1090/noti1489  |doi-access=free|issn=0002-9920}}</ref> She had three brothers and one sister.<ref name="LALord"/>

Clarke attended Dulwich High School for Girls in south London and won a scholarship in 1936, to attend [[Newnham College, Cambridge]]. Her work in an undergraduate geometry class at Cambridge drew the attention of mathematician [[Gordon Welchman]], who became her academic supervisor.

Clarke gained a [[double first]] degree in [[mathematics]] and was a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]].<ref name="ODNB ref">{{cite ODNB|last=Erskine|first=Ralph|title=Murray [Clarke], Joan Elisabeth Lowther (1917–1996)|volume=1|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/71791|access-date=27 October 2013|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/71791|year=2004}}</ref><ref name="BNSobit">{{cite web|url=http://www.britnumsoc.org/publications/Digital%20BNJ/pdfs/1997_BNJ_67_13.pdf|title=Obituary Mrs J.E.L. Murray|last1=Lord Stewartby|year=1997|website=British Numismatic Society|access-date=15 November 2014|archive-date=4 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190804011051/http://www.britnumsoc.org/publications/Digital%20BNJ/pdfs/1997_BNJ_67_13.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> She won the [[Philippa Fawcett|Philippa Fawcett prize]] and was awarded the [[Helen Gladstone]] scholarship for a further year of study.<ref name=":1"/> She was denied a full degree, as until 1948 Cambridge awarded these only to men.<ref name="bbc" />

==Career==
===Codebreaking at Bletchley Park===
Just before the outbreak of World War II, Welchman and three other top mathematicians were recruited to the [[Government Code and Cypher School]], which aimed to break the German Enigma Code. The Germans used the [[Enigma machine]] to encrypt their messages, which they believed to be unbreakable.

In June 1940, [[Gordon Welchman|Welchman]] recruited Clarke to the agency with the offer of 'interesting work'.<ref>{{cite web |author=Anderson, L. V. |date=2014-12-03 |title=The Imitation Game: Fact vs Fiction |url=http://www.slate.com/blogs/browbeat/2014/12/03/the_imitation_game_fact_vs_fiction_how_true_the_new_movie_is_to_alan_turing.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150123222936/http://www.slate.com/blogs/browbeat/2014/12/03/the_imitation_game_fact_vs_fiction_how_true_the_new_movie_is_to_alan_turing.html |archive-date=23 January 2015 |access-date=2015-01-03 |work=Slate}}</ref><ref name="LALord" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Clarke Joan (1917–1996) |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/joan-clarke/ |access-date=2024-05-29 |website=[[English Heritage]] |archive-date=29 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529150829/https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/joan-clarke/ |url-status=live }}</ref> She arrived at [[Bletchley Park]] on 17 June 1940 and was initially placed in an all-women group, referred to as "The Girls", who mainly did routine clerical work. Clarke said she knew of only one other female cryptologist working at Bletchley Park.<ref name="LALord" />

Clarke ended up working at [[Bletchley Park]] in the section known as [[Hut 8]] with [[Alan Turing]], whom she knew slightly through her older brother Michael.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joan Clarke |url=https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/joan-clarke |access-date=2024-05-29 |website=www.gchq.gov.uk |language=en |archive-date=29 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529184108/https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/joan-clarke |url-status=live }}</ref> She quickly became the only female practitioner of [[Banburismus]], a cryptanalytic process developed by [[Alan Turing]] which reduced the need for [[bombe]]s: electromechanical devices as used by British [[cryptologist]]s [[Gordon Welchman|Welchman]] and [[Alan Turing|Turing]] to decipher [[Nazi Germany|German]] [[Enigma machine|encrypted]] messages during [[World War II]].<ref>{{Citation | last = Welchman | first = Gordon | author-link = Gordon Welchman | orig-year = 1997 | year = 2005 | title = The Hut Six story: Breaking the Enigma codes | pages = 138–145 | location = Cleobury Mortimer, England | publisher = M&M Baldwin | isbn = 9780947712341 }} New edition updated with an ''addendum'' consisting of a 1986 paper written by Welchman that corrects his misapprehensions in the 1982 edition.</ref>

In 1941, trawlers were captured as well as their cipher equipment and codes. Before this information was obtained, [[Wolfpack (naval tactic)|wolf packs]] had sunk 282,000 tons of shipping a month from March to June 1941. By November, Clarke and her team were able to reduce this number to 62,000 tons.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Clarke_Joan/|title=Joan Elisabeth Lowther Clarke Murray|website=[[mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk]]|access-date=3 February 2017|archive-date=1 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181001051257/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Clarke_Joan.html|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Conel Hugh O'Donel Alexander|Hugh Alexander]], head of Hut 8 from 1943 to 1944, described her as "one of the best Banburists in the section".<ref name="Burman ref">{{cite thesis | author = Burman, Annie | others = Mikael Byström, Thesis Supervisor, Torkel Jansson, Seminar leader, [Seminar date, 4 June 2013] | year = 2013 | title = Gendering Decryption—Decrypting Gender: The Gender Discourse of Labour at Bletchley Park, 1939–1945 [65 pp.] | type = M.A. | location = Uppsala, SWE | publisher = Uppsala universitet | url = http://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:625771/FULLTEXT01.pdf | access-date = 2017-01-14 | archive-date = 6 October 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141006071736/http://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:625771/FULLTEXT01.pdf | url-status = live }}{{page needed|date=January 2017}}</ref>{{page needed|date=January 2017}} Alexander himself was regarded as the best of the Banburists. He and [[I. J. Good]] considered the process more an intellectual game than a job. It was "not easy enough to be trivial, but not difficult enough to cause a nervous breakdown".<ref>{{Citation | last = Good | first = Jack | author-link = I. J. Good | year = 1993 | contribution = Enigma and Fish | editor-last = Hinsley | editor-first = F.H. | editor-link = Harry Hinsley | editor2-last = Stripp | editor2-first = Alan | title = Codebreakers: The inside story of Bletchley Park | location = [[Oxford]] | publisher = [[Oxford University Press]] | isbn = 978-0-19-280132-6|page=157 |url=https://archive.org/details/codebreakersinsi0000unse |via=[[archive.org]] }}</ref>

An Enigma machine of four rotors was introduced in 1942 which stymied Hut 8's decryption efforts and led to German U-boats successfully attacking Allied shipping convoys again. Clarke had access to intercepted code papers and worked out that that same cipher was used on the fourth rotor as the three-rotor system, which enabled [[Shaun Wylie]] to break the code. Over a million German naval messages were decrypted from the Enigma machines by Hut 8.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Sherwood |first=Harriet |date=2024-05-29 |title=Bletchley Park codebreaker Joan Clarke honoured with blue plaque |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/may/29/bletchley-park-codebreaker-joan-clarke-honoured-with-blue-plaque |access-date=2024-05-29 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

In the period before [[Normandy landings|D-Day]], Hut 8's work increased, as the team worked in conjunction with [[Bletchley Park|Hut 10.]] Their work involved decoding German weather signals, enabling Allied bombing raids in the time prior to the Normandy Landings. Their work also supported the [[Special Operations Executive]] operations which laid groundworks for the invasion.<ref name=":1" />

Clarke became deputy head of Hut 8 in 1944,<ref name="Burman ref" /><ref name="bletchleyparkresearch/women-codebreakers"/> although she was prevented from progressing because she was female, and she was paid less than the men.<ref name=":2" /><ref name="LALord"/> A pay rise was arranged and she was promoted to [[Linguist]] even though she spoke no other language.<ref name="bletchleyparkresearch/women-codebreakers">{{cite web |title=Women Codebreakers |url=https://www.bletchleyparkresearch.co.uk/research-notes/women-codebreakers/ |website=Bletchley Park Research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729122332/https://www.bletchleyparkresearch.co.uk/research-notes/women-codebreakers/ |archive-date=Jul 29, 2020 |date=3 October 2013}}</ref>

<blockquote>In order to be paid for her promotion, Clarke needed to be classed as a linguist, as Civil Service bureaucracy had no protocols in place for a senior female cryptanalyst. She would later take great pleasure in filling in forms with the line: "grade: linguist, languages: none".<ref name="bbc"/> -[[BBC News]]</blockquote>

=== Relationship with Turing ===
<blockquote>"Naturally, that worried me a bit, because I did know that was something which was almost certainly permanent, but we carried on".<ref name="bbc"/> – Joan Clarke</blockquote>
Clarke and Turing had been close friends since soon after they met, and continued to be until Turing's death in 1954. They shared many hobbies and had similar personalities.<ref name="bbc" /> They became very good friends at Bletchley Park. Turing arranged their shifts so they could work together, and they also spent much of their free time together. In early 1941, Turing proposed marriage to Clarke,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-13 |title=Research uncovers secrets of Newnham women sent to codebreak at Bletchley |url=https://newn.cam.ac.uk/newnham-news/research-uncovers-secrets-of-newnham-women-sent-to-codebreak-at-bletchley-park#:~:text=More%20than%2070%20former%20students%20of%20Newnham |access-date=2024-10-03 |website=newn.cam.ac.uk |language=en |archive-date=7 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007091617/https://newn.cam.ac.uk/newnham-news/research-uncovers-secrets-of-newnham-women-sent-to-codebreak-at-bletchley-park#:~:text=More%20than%2070%20former%20students%20of%20Newnham |url-status=live }}</ref> and subsequently introduced her to his family. When he privately admitted his homosexuality to her, she was reportedly unfazed by the revelation. After a holiday in Wales, Turing decided that he could not go through with the marriage, and broke up with Clarke in mid-1941. Clarke later admitted that she had suspected Turing's homosexuality for some time, and it was not much of a surprise when he made the admission to her.<ref name="Times 29 July 1952" /><ref name="FreeBMD" />

== Postwar ==
Joan Clarke was awarded an [[Order of the British Empire|MBE]] for her codebreaking activities in 1946.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> After the war, Clarke worked for [[Government Communications Headquarters]] (GCHQ). There, in 1947, she met Lieutenant-Colonel John Kenneth Ronald Murray, a retired army officer who had served in India. They were married by the [[Bishop of Chichester]] on 26 July 1952 in [[Chichester Cathedral]], where her father was a [[Canon (priest)|Canon]].<ref name="Times 29 July 1952">{{cite news| title= Births, marriages, and deaths| newspaper= [[The Times]]| date= 29 July 1952| page= 1 }}</ref><ref name= "FreeBMD">{{cite web| url= https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/search.pl?start=1952&end=1952&sq=3&eq=3&type=Marriages&vol=5h&pgno=937&db=bmd_1578958416&jsexec=1&mono=0&v=MTU4MDczMjMwMjpmMjY3NzIxNzZjMjZhZmJkYTIyOGE0YTdhNmM0MzZiZGQ0Y2M1MWI5&searchdef=eq%3D4%26sq%3D1%26surname%3DMurray%26end%3D1970%26districtid%3D1056%26db%3Dbmd_1578958416%26given%3DJohn%26type%3DMarriages%26start%3D1940&action=Find| title= Index entry| access-date= 3 February 2020| work= [[FreeBMD]]| publisher= [[Office for National Statistics]]| archive-date= 11 September 2021| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210911141555/https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/search.pl?start=1952&end=1952&sq=3&eq=3&type=Marriages&vol=5h&pgno=937&db=bmd_1578958416&jsexec=1&mono=0&v=MTU4MDczMjMwMjpmMjY3NzIxNzZjMjZhZmJkYTIyOGE0YTdhNmM0MzZiZGQ0Y2M1MWI5&searchdef=eq%3D4%26sq%3D1%26surname%3DMurray%26end%3D1970%26districtid%3D1056%26db%3Dbmd_1578958416%26given%3DJohn%26type%3DMarriages%26start%3D1940&action=Find| url-status= live}}</ref> Shortly after their marriage, John Murray retired from GCHQ due to ill health and the couple moved to [[Crail]] in [[Fife]]<ref name="BNSobit"/> where they lived at Priorscroft, 14 Nethergate.<ref>{{cite book| last=Murray| first=John| author-link=John Kenneth Ronald Murray | title=A Crail Scrapbook| publisher=Crail Museum Trust| year=2010| location=Crail}}</ref> In 1962, they returned to work at GCHQ, where Clarke would work until retiring in 1977 at the age of 60.<ref name="LALord">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Clarke_Joan/|title=Joan Elisabeth Lowther Clarke Murray|work=Honours project|publisher=University of St Andrews|last=Lord|first=Lynsey Ann|year=2008|access-date=2013-11-05|archive-date=1 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181001051257/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Clarke_Joan.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.britnumsoc.org/publications/Digital%20BNJ/pdfs/1986_BNJ_56_13.pdf|title=Obituary: Lieutenant-Colonel J.K.R. Murray|publisher=[[British Numismatic Society]]|volume=56|pages=201–203|journal=British Numismatic Journal|last=Stewart|first=Ian|year=1986|access-date=2013-11-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916040652/http://www.britnumsoc.org/publications/Digital%20BNJ/pdfs/1986_BNJ_56_13.pdf|archive-date=16 September 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

After her husband's death in 1986, Clarke moved to [[Headington]], Oxfordshire, where she continued her research into [[Numismatics|coinage]]. During the 1980s, she helped [[Harry Hinsley|Sir Harry Hinsley]] with the appendix to Volume 3, Part 2 of ''[[History of the Second World War#Intelligence|British Intelligence in the Second World War]]''.<ref name="ODNB ref">{{cite ODNB|last=Erskine|first=Ralph|title=Murray [Clarke], Joan Elisabeth Lowther (1917–1996)|volume=1|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/71791|access-date=27 October 2013|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/71791|year=2004}}</ref> She also helped historians studying war-time codebreaking at Bletchley Park. Due to continuing secrecy among cryptanalysts, the full extent of her accomplishments remains unknown.<ref name="LALord"/> Recent histories of GCHQ suggest that she played a role in its work during the [[Falklands War]]: helping to track the Argentine submarine ''[[ARA Santa Fe (S-21)|Santa Fe]]'' in April 1982.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ferris |first=John |title=Behind the enigma: the authorised history of GCHQ, Britain´s Secret Cyber-Intelligence Agency |date=2021 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-5266-0546-7 |location=London Oxford New York New Delhi Sydney}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hannigan |first=Robert |title=Counter-intelligence: what the secret world can teach us about problem-solving and creativity |date=2024 |publisher=HarperCollins Publishers |isbn=978-0-00-839855-2 |location=London Dublin |pages=147}}</ref>

===Numismatic interest===
After meeting her husband, who had published work on the Scottish coinage of the 16th and 17th centuries, Clarke developed an interest in [[numismatic]]s history.<ref name=":0"/> She established the sequence of the complex series of [[Unicorn (coin)|gold unicorn]] and heavy [[groat (coin)|groat]] coins that were in circulation [[Scottish coinage|in Scotland]] during the reigns of [[James III of Scotland|James III]] and [[James IV of Scotland|James IV]]. In 1986, her research was recognised by the [[British Numismatic Society]] when she was awarded the Sanford Saltus Gold Medal. Issue No. 405 of the ''[[Numismatic Circular]]'' described her paper on the topic as "magisterial".<ref name="ODNB ref"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britnumsoc.org/mpandf/sanfordsaltus.shtml|title=Sanford Saltus Gold Medal|year=2013|website=British Numismatic Society|access-date=2014-11-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112055541/http://britnumsoc.org/mpandf/sanfordsaltus.shtml|archive-date=12 November 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Death==
Clarke died at her home at 7 Larkfields, [[Headington Quarry]], [[Oxford]], England on 4 September 1996 at age 79.<ref name="LALord"/>

== Commemoration ==
[[File:JOAN CLARKE 1917–1996 Code-breaker lived here.jpg|thumb|275x275px|[[English Heritage]] [[blue plaque]] for Joan Clarke<ref name=":1"/>]]
An [[Oxfordshire Blue Plaque]] was unveiled on her house on 27 July 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joan Clarke Murray and Headington |url=https://www.headington.org.uk/history/famous_people/clarke_joan.html |access-date=2024-05-29 |website=www.headington.org.uk |archive-date=29 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529181105/https://www.headington.org.uk/history/famous_people/clarke_joan.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.oxonblueplaques.org.uk/plaques/murray_joan.html | publisher=[[Oxfordshire Blue Plaques Board]] | title=Joan Murray, née Clarke (1917–1996) Cryptanalyst and numismatist – 7 Larkfields, Headington Quarry, Oxford | location=UK | access-date=27 June 2020 | archive-date=30 May 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200530010704/http://www.oxonblueplaques.org.uk/plaques/murray_joan.html | url-status=live }}</ref>

In May 2024 a [[blue plaque]] in Joan Clarke's memory was unveiled by [[English Heritage]] at 193 Rosendale Road, [[West Dulwich]], London, SE21 8LW, her home as a child.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sheridan |first=Danielle |date=2024-05-29 |title=Keira Knightley's Imitation Game character to receive Blue Plaque |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/05/29/keira-knightley-imitation-game-blue-plaque/ |access-date=2024-05-29 |work=The Telegraph |language=en-GB |issn=0307-1235 |archive-date=29 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240529181104/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/05/29/keira-knightley-imitation-game-blue-plaque/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Portrayal in adaptation==
Clarke was portrayed by [[Keira Knightley]] in the film ''[[The Imitation Game]]'' (2014), opposite [[Benedict Cumberbatch]] as [[Alan Turing]].<ref name="bbc"/><ref name=HodgesCrit>{{cite web|url=http://www.pinknews.co.uk/2013/06/24/alan-turings-biographer-criticises-upcoming-biopic-for-downplaying-gay-identity/|title=Alan Turing's biographer criticises upcoming biopic for downplaying gay identity|date=24 June 2013|publisher=PinkNews.co.uk|access-date=18 November 2014|archive-date=27 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130627212110/http://www.pinknews.co.uk/2013/06/24/alan-turings-biographer-criticises-upcoming-biopic-for-downplaying-gay-identity/|url-status=live}}</ref> Turing's surviving niece, Inagh Payne, described Clarke as "rather plain" and thought that Knightley was inappropriately cast as Clarke.<ref name="RadioTimes">{{cite web|url=http://www.radiotimes.com/news/2013-11-19/benedict-cumberbatch-and-keira-knightleys-imitation-game-romance-labelled-inaccurate|title=Imitation Game filmmakers accused of romanticising the relationship between Benedict Cumberbatch and Keira Knightley's characters by Alan Turing's niece, Inagh Payne|first=Susanna|last=Lazarus|work=Radio Times|date=19 November 2013|access-date=2014-09-10|archive-date=21 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131121005413/http://www.radiotimes.com/news/2013-11-19/benedict-cumberbatch-and-keira-knightleys-imitation-game-romance-labelled-inaccurate|url-status=live}}</ref> Turing biographer [[Andrew Hodges]] also criticised the film, stating the script "built up the relationship with Joan much more than it actually was".<ref name=HodgesCrit/> Knightley however was nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress]] at the [[87th Academy Awards]] for her performance as Clarke.<ref name="BBCOscars">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/entertainment-arts-30834325|title=Oscars 2015: Best supporting actress|work=BBC News|date=23 February 2015|archive-date=11 September 2021|access-date=9 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210911141555/https://www.bbc.com/news/entertainment-arts-30834325|url-status=live}} Retrieved on 2019-04-09</ref>

In contrast, an article by BBC journalist Joe Miller said that Clarke's "story has been immortalised". Director [[Morten Tyldum]] said the film shows how Clarke succeeded in her field despite working in a time "when intelligence wasn't really appreciated in women".<ref name=bbc/>

[[Amanda Root]] plays a character based on Clarke, renamed and recharacterized as ''Patricia ('Pat') Green'', in the 1996 film ''[[Breaking the Code (film)|Breaking the Code]]''.<ref name="worcesternews/25410951">{{cite news |title=The secret life of Joan: wartime codebreaker and cryptanalyst |url=https://www.worcesternews.co.uk/news/25410951.joan-clarke-bletchley-park-codebreakers-ww2/ |access-date=19 November 2025 |work=[[Worcester News]] |date=24 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250901062426/https://www.worcesternews.co.uk/news/25410951.joan-clarke-bletchley-park-codebreakers-ww2/ |archive-date=September 1, 2025 |language=en}}</ref><!-- {{cn|date=November 2025}} -->
